vignette:
George was seventy-three years old, a retired journalist who had spent decades covering urban conflict, but nothing had prepared him for the morning of the City Market bombing. He had arrived early to photograph the crowd for a human-interest piece. The detonation came from a parked delivery van-a man-made disaster, he would later learn, orchestrated by a fringe group. In the seconds after the blast, George saw limbs and debris rising, tasted the thick, metallic tang of blood and the acrid burn of explosives settling on his tongue. He helped drag survivors from the rubble until emergency crews arrived, then filed his report, including the photos he had taken. In the weeks that followed, he tried to move on, but the memory refused to fade. The taste-sharp, coppery, chemical-returned unexpectedly when he bit into certain foods, and he began avoiding anything that might trigger that sensory echo. His own photographs, published widely in newspapers, became unbearable; he could no longer look at images of crowds or even news coverage of other disasters without feeling the ground shift beneath him.

At first, George told himself the reaction was normal, that he would settle back into routine. But he started to notice small changes in how he moved through the world. In his apartment, he sat only with his back against a wall, positioned so he could see every doorway. He began listening-really listening-for sounds that might mean someone was entering his home: the creak of a floorboard, the faint turn of a lock. In public, his eyes scanned tables for knives, for glass bottles, for anything that could become a weapon. Unpredictable situations-a car backfiring, a sudden shout-made him freeze completely, stuck in place until his heart slowed. He became certain that if he let himself think about the bombing in any detail, he would fall apart, so he pushed the thoughts down, tried to keep his mind busy. That was when the spending started: he bought expensive camera equipment he did not need, then furniture, then clothes, charging thousands of dollars to his credit card in a kind of urgent, hollow rush that temporarily drowned out the replays in his head. The replays were the worst-a film that looped without permission, showing the same bodies, the same smoke, the same faces, until he felt as though it was happening right then, in his living room, his body braced for impact. And yet, when the feeling passed, the memories seemed unreal, too extreme to have happened to him; sometimes he wondered if he had imagined the whole thing.

Over the months and years, George became a ghost in his own life. His divorce, years before the event, had already left him isolated, but now he found it impossible to connect with his adult daughter or his few remaining friends. He had lost the capacity for normal emotions, he believed-nothing felt genuine anymore, and when he tried to laugh or care, the sensation was flat, distant. He retired early, not because he needed to but because nothing in his work felt meaningful. The stories he had spent a lifetime chasing now seemed empty, and he questioned what he had ever been trying to accomplish. He stopped answering phone calls. He stopped going to restaurants because the unpredictability of the environment was too much-people walking behind him, sudden noises from the kitchen-and even his own home no longer felt safe, because he could not relax anywhere, not even when he locked the doors.

What finally brought George to seek help was his daughter, who visited after a long silence and found him sitting in the dark, his back to the wall, staring at nothing. She told him she was frightened for him. He agreed to see a therapist, not because he believed it would work, but because he could no longer stand the numbness. He told the clinician he wanted to feel something real again, even if that meant facing the memories he had worked so hard to avoid. But what he feared most was that the moment he started to let the memories in, they would swallow him whole, and he would never find his way back.
